previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of chronic right lower quadrant abdominal pain, diabetic gastroparesis, hypertension, and depression was admitted due to an acute worsening of abdominal pain, nausea, and poor oral intake. Her vital signs were stable, and physical exam revealed only mild right lower quadrant tenderness. Laboratory tests, including CBC, metabolic panel, liver enzymes, and lipase, were normal. Given her recent negative imaging and stable condition, no additional radiology was performed. She improved with IV fluids, pain control, and transition back to her oral medications, including ondansetron and metoclopramide for nausea. Her diabetes and blood pressure remained well-controlled. She was discharged home with instructions to continue her home regimen and follow up with her primary care provider, gastroenterologist, psychiatrist, and pain clinic.

radiology_notes.text:
CLINICAL HISTORY:  Headache, evaluate mass and ?cavernous sinus thrombosis.

TECHNIQUE:  MRI brain without contrast and MRV without contrast.  According to
the technologist's note, the patient was falling asleep, medicated due to
claustrophobia and scanning was repeatedly performed to obtain the best
possible images.  Sagittal T1, axial FLAIR, T2, gradient echo and 2D
time-of-flight MRV, with 3D MIP-reconstructions.
 
COMPARISON:  MRI ___.

FINDINGS:

There is no intracranial hemorrhage, mass, mass effect, shift of midline
structures or signs of acute infarction.  As seen on the earlier study, there
are FLAIR-hyperintensities more in the central pons than in the
periventricular and subcortical white matter, not significantly changed,
likely related to chronic small vessel ischemic disease.  The ventricles and
sulcal configuration are normal.  The visualized paranasal sinuses are clear.

MRV:  The dural venous sinuses are patent without evidence of dural sinus or
other cerebral venous thrombosis.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No acute intracranial process.

2.  Chronic small vessel ischemic disease, unchanged since the earlier study,
predominantly with involvement of the central pons.

3.  Normal MRV without evidence of cerebral venous thrombosis.

N.B. Though there is no finding to suggest cavernous sinus thrombosis, this
would be better-assessed with enhanced thin-section MR study, targeted to the
skull base, or CTA.
